text: A child works out early that a face can be put on like a coat, and then wears it into adulthood. Genjiro Arato gives that arrangement 134 minutes, which is long enough to feel the labour in it: the young man at the centre is not misunderstood so much as permanently on duty, performing an ordinary person for a society that declines to take him seriously in any case. Drink and the rest follow, less as rebellion than as upkeep — a way of getting the costume back on in the morning. The patience is deliberate; no single incident is going to resolve a habit formed that early. What holds the attention is smaller and stranger than despair: the sustained effort of an act performed for an audience that was never especially watching.

Francisco turns thirty in a cowboy costume, at a children's party, surrounded by children he hates. Miguel Gomes takes a piece of folk wisdom that comes with a deadline — until thirty the face is God's doing, after that it is yours — and treats the deadline as though it were enforceable. The premise reaches us in the voice of somebody telling Francisco off, all imperatives and repeat-after-me, which is a strange way to address a man of thirty and evidently the correct one. Carnival supplies the costume; the fantasy licence gives the birthday teeth. Thirty is not usually a deadline, but it is here. What comes of 108 minutes is a comedy about being found out on schedule, staged in a room where everyone else is a head shorter and better behaved than he is.

Murder hands a young lawyer his first large case, and the case turns out to have older business inside it. Marco Kreuzpaintner's 2019 film wears a thriller label, but the machinery is legal: 118 minutes in which a single matter keeps enlarging under the hands of somebody with no standing to hold it. A conspiracy of any size implies people who once did the work of settling things, and who have no interest in doing it twice. That is the pressure here — not danger exactly, but the quiet preference of an entire profession for a colleague who asks fewer questions. His inexperience cuts both ways: he does not know which requests are unusual, and so he makes them. The killing is brutal, and it is the smallest thing in the film.

Toma loves Ana, and loving Ana becomes a kind of work that keeps no hours. Călin Peter Netzer starts them as students in a literature faculty — two people generously supplied with words for what they feel — and then gives 127 minutes to everything those words cannot manage. Ana is ill; the relationship comes apart slowly, which is the harder version to film, since nothing decisive happens on any particular Tuesday and the damage only accumulates. Care and love get tangled early and stay tangled. A couple can go years without establishing which of the two is holding things up, and the film seems less interested in diagnosing Ana than in watching the pair negotiate, day by day, an arrangement neither of them agreed to in the seminar room.

Hyun-woo leaves prison after seventeen years, and the country outside has had all that time to rearrange itself without consulting him. Im Sang-soo sends him back to the village where he once hid as a fugitive, which puts two stretches of time in the same frame: the return now, and the months when a woman named Yoon-hee gave him a room and her company. Conviction is cheap to declare and expensive to keep, and part of this bill was paid by somebody who was not the activist. At 112 minutes it is as much a love story as a political one, and the two do not separate cleanly. What it goes back to is not the movement as it appears in speeches but a particular house and the ordinary business of hiding a man inside it.

A civil service exam is a door with a fixed number of places behind it, and the waiting costs money. Kim Joong-hyun spends 112 minutes with Min-kyung, who is preparing for one, and the preparation turns out to be the smaller half of her day; the rest goes to the ordinary expense of staying in the city long enough to sit the thing. Films about examinations tend to organise themselves around the result. This one is built the other way round, on the season before it, when study and survival compete for the same hours and the same coins. Nothing in that arrangement is dramatic on any single day, which is precisely where the pressure comes from: the days are interchangeable, they cost the same as each other, and there are only so many of them left.

A retainer kills himself to make a crime public, and the crime stays private anyway. That is where Eiichi Kudō begins in 1963: a lord who kills with impunity because he is the Shogun's younger brother, a promotion pending that will extend his reach, and an official silence no lawful instrument can break. The reply is arithmetic — twelve men and the strategist who leads them, against a defending force commanded by his match, a man assigned to protect somebody he despises. Both are doing their duty, which makes the symmetry uncomfortable. Killing at those odds is a problem of arrangement long before it is a problem of swords, and 125 minutes leaves the arranging room to become as tense as whatever it is arranging.

Two poets marry, which means two people who will each be writing it down. Christine Jeffs holds her film to that single relationship — Ted Hughes and Sylvia Plath, 109 minutes, no survey of the collected works — and the narrowness is the interesting decision. A marriage between people in the same trade has its own weather: the same rooms, the same hours, the same small supply of attention, and work that cannot be left at an office. Whatever biography sits behind it, what has to be staged is domestic: talk, ambition, the way praise for one person lands in a house containing two. The result is nearer a chamber drama than a life story, and it takes the poets seriously as spouses before it takes them seriously as poets.
